positions.commentary: The speaker believes Dollar General is perfectly weathered for a deflationary environment.
The speaker notes that Amazon's business has been up during the crisis, which is remarkable.
The speaker highlights that Microsoft's cloud business, Azure, has been up during the crisis.
The speaker suggests that owning the five big tech companies plus Visa and MasterCard would have been sufficient.

The speaker thinks Exxon is fine if oil returns to $45-$50 sustainably, but notes their reserves are overstated using a longer term higher oil price, and they are not businesses you can own durably for 30 years because they destroy capital.
The speaker mentions adding Olin Corporation to a small position which they have since made into a material position for the firm.
The speaker notes the end game is probably hyperinflation given where we are, but we will go through various iterations of what the Japanese have done.
The speaker notes Berkshire took their Southwest Airlines and their Delta positions below 10%.
The speaker regrets selling PepsiCo because it is perfectly situated with pricing power and a command position in distribution.
The speaker expresses concern that if governments commandeer assets in China, Starbucks stores could be kicked out, making the company not worth mid-20s to earnings.
The speaker predicts that if capacity utilization drops to 85% in two or three years, it will be a game changer impacting companies selling into the supply chain.
The speaker mentions Nike as an example of a company that moved production to Vietnam and then China.
The speaker believes Costco is a great business but the current valuation is too high, trading at 40 times earnings compared to a fair number of 25.

thesis: This episode argues that while the five major tech companies and Visa/MasterCard formed a sufficient portfolio during the crisis, investors must scrutinize cyclical businesses like ExxonMobil and Olin for their destructive capital allocation and unsustainable dividend policies. It suggests that durable ownership is difficult in sectors where companies are handcuffed by high payouts and debt, even if they appear fine at specific oil price recoveries.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Amazon's business has been up during the crisis, which is remarkable.
claims.quote: You think about Amazon's business being up during a crisis, that's happened.

claims.claim: The speaker highlights that Microsoft's cloud business, Azure, has been up during the crisis.
claims.quote: Microsoft's cloud business, Azure, being up during the crisis.

claims.claim: The speaker suggests that owning the five big tech companies plus Visa and MasterCard would have been sufficient.
claims.quote: And maybe you throw in a Visa and a MasterCard, so seven businesses. If you'd only own those five or seven, that's all you needed.

claims.claim: The speaker states they have a good history of buying ExxonMobil when they thought it was cheap.
claims.quote: We've owned ExxonMobil, cyclically. We, I think, have a good history buying it when we thought it was cheap, selling it when it was

claims.claim: The speaker owns the stock but notes the business has eroded over the last 10 years, is handcuffed by a high dividend payout, and is a capital destroyer, though they think they are fine if oil returns to $45-$50.
claims.quote: We've owned ExxonMobil, cyclically. We, I think, have a good history buying it when we thought it was cheap, selling it when it was dear. The problem with oil is, and the world learned this lesson in our hurry here this quarter, with OPEC, really existing in perpetuity with a sword over the head of the industry.

claims.claim: The speaker notes Exxon has increased dividends in perpetuity to the point where they haven't earned them recently, are borrowing money to pay them, and have significant debt, but owns the stock and thinks they are fine if oil prices recover.
claims.quote: And over the last 10 years, they've been hitched this dividend policy. And they've just increased the dividends in perpetuity to the point where in the last couple of years, they've not earned the dividend. If you're the CEO of a business that is hitched to a high dividend payout, it's absolute handcuffs.

claims.claim: The speaker states Exxon has a dividend of $3.48 a share this year but didn't earn it for the last four years, is hitched to a payout rate over 100% of capital, and has $70 billion in debt.
claims.quote: In Exxon's case, they've got a dividend that's going to be $3.48.48 a share this year, but they didn't even earn that last year. They didn't earn it the year before. They didn't earn it the year before that. They didn't earn it the year before that. They're hitched to a payout rate that's over 100% of their capital.

claims.claim: The speaker notes Exxon cut its CAPX budget by 30% but hasn't touched the dividend, and while they think they are fine if oil returns to $45-$50, they are not businesses you can own durably for 30 years because they destroy capital.
claims.quote: They cut the CAPX budget by 30% a couple weeks ago, but they haven't touched the dumb dividend. So we did a deep dive on a bunch of little independent oil and gas companies last year because this crisis didn't just start. These businesses and the service sector in particular has been incredibly weak.

claims.claim: The speaker thinks Exxon is fine if oil returns to $45-$50 sustainably, but notes their reserves are overstated using a longer term higher oil price, and they are not businesses you can own durably for 30 years because they destroy capital.
claims.quote: But if we get oil back to, say, $45 to $45 to $50 sustainably, Exxon's in good shape. When they calculate the reserves, they're overstated, using a longer term higher oil price. But I think they're fine. At today's prices, you'll wind up making a lot of money. But they are not businesses, Patrick, you can own durably for 30 years.

claims.claim: The speaker compares Olin to Exxon, noting Olin is in the same boat regarding high dividends, recommends cutting the dividend during the crisis, and calls it one of the stupidest things you can have because you're obligated as a cyclical business to always pay the dumb dividend.
claims.quote: Olin's in that same boat. My recommendation to the folks that run Olin has been during this crisis, you've got to cut the dividend. It's 80 cents a share. They're in the list of the dividend aristocrats, which is one of the stupidest things you can have because you're obligated as a cyclical business to always pay the dumb dividend.

claims.claim: The speaker notes Olin's dividend is $120 million, they ought to be freeing up but haven't, and they are obligated as a cyclical business to always pay the dumb dividend.
claims.quote: Well, in Olin's case, that's $120 million. They ought to be freeing up, but they haven't freed up. In Exxon's case, they've got a dividend that's going to be $3.48.48 a share this year, but they didn't even earn that last year.

claims.claim: The speaker notes Berkshire has been extremely quiet in the COVID period, has taken positions below 10% in airlines and money center banks, and has a huge cash pile, but there is very little activity to observe yet.
claims.quote: Well, there's very little activity to observe yet, because to your point, they've been extremely quiet. I think the 08 crisis evolved over a longer duration. And so when companies like Goldman and GE needed capital, you didn't have the massive federal intervention immediately like you've had had in this crisis.

claims.claim: The speaker notes Berkshire has shrunk their bank in the York position to 10%, which was really regulatory driven, and they own a couple suppliers of parts to airlines which are good businesses but they are struggling with what the back-end curve looks like.
claims.quote: Just last week, they shrunk their bank in the York position to 10%, which was really regulatory driven in that case. So it's hard to know what's going on inside the business. I think you've not seen the deals like they did during the crisis yet because of the noability of this federal money that's coming to the party.

claims.claim: The speaker notes Berkshire took their Southwest Airlines and their Delta positions below 10%.
claims.quote: You saw them take their Southwest Airlines and their Delta positions below 10%. Just last week, they shrunk their bank in the York position to 10%, which was really regulatory driven in that case.

claims.claim: The speaker believes Dollar General is perfectly weathered for a deflationary environment.
claims.quote: I go back to portfolio companies like Dollar General, which I think is perfectly weathered for a deflationary environment, except that if the overall cost level, cost of good, sold, declined by 2%, you're going to be pushing back on wages by 2% to try to maintain margins.

claims.claim: The speaker regrets selling PepsiCo because it is perfectly situated with pricing power and a command position in distribution.
claims.quote: I regret now having owned and sold PepsiCo a few years ago because a company like that is perfectly situated. Their beverage franchise, but also their salty snacks. PepsiCo still is a business that has pricing power.

claims.claim: The speaker owns Starbucks but has a major concern that Chinese governments might commandeer their stores in China.
claims.quote: I think about companies like Starbucks. We've always said we would never directly own a Chinese business. And so Luckin, a couple weeks ago, had a lot of people laughing unless you own the company. But we own Starbucks. Starbucks is a top five holding of bars.

claims.claim: The speaker predicts that if capacity utilization drops to 85% in two or three years, it will be a game changer impacting companies selling into the supply chain.
claims.quote: Well, if we're going to wind up with 85% of capacity utilization two or three years from now, all of these new aircraft that have been built, it's a game changer. So that really impacts companies that sell into the supply chain, that, you know, that sell into the parts business for replacement.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions Nike as an example of a company that moved production to Vietnam and then China.
claims.quote: I've watched the economy for the 30 years that I've managed money, move production to the lowest cost of production. So Nike move production to Vietnam. And then as Vietnam grew they moved production to China.

claims.claim: The speaker believes Costco is a great business but the current valuation is too high, trading at 40 times earnings compared to a fair number of 25.
claims.quote: I think at some point Costco trades at 25 times. The growth curve is not what it was when we bought the stock for the first time in 2000.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions adding Olin Corporation to a small position which they have since made into a material position for the firm.
claims.quote: One, Olin Corporation, which we brought into a small position and it was the price to climb this year. We've really made it a material position for the firm.

claims.claim: The speaker notes it is hard to know what Berkshire has done with its $125 billion in cash, but expects they bought back shares.
claims.quote: My expectation would be of the $125 billion in cash that they would have bought back a whole bunch of shares.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions Berkshire spent around $7 or $8 billion last year buying back stock.
claims.quote: They spent on the order of $7 or $8 billion last year buying stock back average of $202 or $203 on the B shares.

claims.claim: The speaker presumes Berkshire has spent a fair amount of capital, but it will be interesting to see what they've done on the equity front.
claims.quote: I'm probably, I could be wrong, but I presume they've spent a fair amount of capitalists. It's going to be interesting on the equity front to see what they've done.

claims.claim: The speaker notes it is hard to know what Berkshire has done with its portfolio, specifically regarding banks and airlines.
claims.quote: But it's hard to know what Berkshire has done. It's going to be really interesting to see. My expectation would be of the $125 billion in cash that they would have bought back a whole bunch of shares.

claims.claim: The speaker suggests Berkshire might have sold down the airline structure knowing demand will not return to 2019 levels.
claims.quote: I wouldn't be surprised to see Berkshire having sold out or materially sold down the airline structure knowing that this will not be the same business going forward, knowing that demand will not return to 100% of 2019 levels.

claims.claim: The speaker notes it is hard to know if Berkshire has sold down banks, as the banks seem to be in more trouble than the world thought.
claims.quote: I don't know if they've sold down banks. The banks seem to be in more trouble than the world thought. They had to meet Graham Dodd standards and they apparently were better capitalized.

claims.claim: The speaker questions if Berkshire's cash is invested in T-bills, noting nobody does that.
claims.quote: So Berkshers goes into the year with $125 billion in cash, but what's their cash investor then, T-bills? Nobody does that.

claims.claim: The speaker describes Berkshire as a crazy time for such an interesting company and looks forward to seeing buyback activity.
claims.quote: It's a crazy time for such an interesting company. I can't wait to see the buyback activity looking back now once we get the data.

claims.claim: The speaker notes Berkshire owns Saratage and Simon property, which are long-term businesses that are probably going to zero.
claims.quote: The mall retailers, even Mr. Buffett is invested in, at least he was investing in Saratage, first Simon property, all of the big malls, just long-term businesses that are probably going to zero in a lot of cases are still cheap.

claims.claim: The speaker contends that coming out the backside of this, there will be deflation for an ordinarily long period of time.
claims.quote: I think a better way to think about what to do with capital today is think about how capital is going to work for the next 10 or 20 years, certainly for the next 10 years. And if you bake in short-term interest rates, which are already at the zero bound, if you bake in a Federal Reserve that will be determined to try to compress long-term treasury rates as close to the zero bound as possible, and

claims.claim: The speaker notes Berkshire owns companies that are the right businesses and adding to them has been the right thing to do.
claims.quote: And so, yeah, I think the companies that we own are the right businesses. And to the extent we've been able to add to those, it's been the right thing to do.

claims.claim: The speaker notes the end game is probably hyperinflation given where we are, but we will go through various iterations of what the Japanese have done.
claims.quote: The end game is probably hyperinflation, given where we are. Because here and abroad, there's simply too much on balance cheap debt. But we will go through various iterations of what the Japanese have done.
